criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design. Discusses context of ethical issues in engineering organisations. Identifies the relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Identifies several issues (end-user harm, professional responsibility, product quality versus competitiveness) and names key stakeholders. Context in engineering organisations is touched on (rapidly growing, competitive industry). The link to engineering design and QA process is thin, and stakeholder interests are not developed in the introduction, so it falls short of Excellent.

evidence.quote: The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions of the ethical issues. Draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Presents three arguments for shipping and three against, with reasonable depth for the against side (EACE clauses, HSSIB case, VW case). The for side is thinner and partly speculative. Conclusions are drawn, but recommendations target mainly Rachel and her company; the chip contract company and health department's needs are not weighed in decision recommendations.

evidence.quote: Shipping potentially defective products is not an ethical way to conduct business.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument, which justifies the conclusion. The body of the report follows a logical structure, with paragraphs linked and content ordered in a way that is easy to follow and support the building of the argument. Arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logical flow from for/against discussion to ethical path to conclusion and recommendations, and the arguments support the conclusion. Argument is persuasive. Systematic treatment of all stakeholders is incomplete, and some claims (job loss, competitor behaviour) are asserted rather than argued, so not Excellent.

evidence.quote: the decision to Not Ship is certainly the most ethical path.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence. Research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Four references, two real-world case studies (NHS/HSSIB, Volkswagen) and the EACE code, give some substantiation. Little quantitative evidence and no peer-reviewed or industry-technical sources. The CNBC source is a marketing article and does not support the claimed Samsung/Google comparison. Research depth is moderate.

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections which serve their respective functions well: abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion. Maps, figures, tables, and any visual elements are correctly used to support written discussions. The writing is free from any grammatical errors. The expression is fluent, has appropriate word choice, is concise, easy to read and understand. References are well-structured and appropriate providing strong support of the motivations in the report.
criteria.reasoning: Sections are clearly structured with abstract, intro, body, conclusion and references. However there are several grammatical and typographical errors ('DICUSSION', 'Actin', 'of professional'), no figures or tables, and reference entries are inconsistent or incomplete (missing URL, garbled author). Language is not error-free, so Satisfactory fits.

technical_issues.issue: Overstates causation: the HSSIB findings relate to IT failures contributing to harm, but the text states the malfunction scenario 'led to deaths' without qualification.

technical_issues.where: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship
technical_issues.issue: Apple/Samsung/Google competitive claim is supported only by a CNBC marketing article that does not address rivals; the citation does not substantiate the argument.
Volkswagen case involved deliberate defeat devices (intentional fraud), which is a weak analogy for shipping known defects under time pressure; the distinction is not discussed.

EACE clause 2.3b (outside competence) is misapplied to the QA timeframe; the clause concerns qualifications and experience, not schedule constraints. Clause references should be verified against the code.
Does not address the scenario's distinction between physical-harm failures (never shipped) and data-loss failures (shipped), nor a practical rule for when Rachel may ship known defects.
Reference formats are inconsistent and incomplete: BBC entry lacks URL; NYT entry has garbled author names and a broken access date; the word count may exceed the 1,500 limit.

overall: Solid, mostly ethical reasoning with clear stakeholder identification and a justified recommendation. Weaknesses: thin evidence and weak source alignment, causation overstated, no actionable decision rule for shipping known defects, several language errors, no visuals, and inconsistent references. Approximate total 34/50.

feedback.summary: You have written a clear, mostly ethical report with a justified recommendation not to ship. Your stakeholder identification and the contrast between the arguments for and against shipping are strengths. To move up, sharpen your evidence, qualify some of your claims, and tighten your language and referencing. The next steps below focus on these areas.
next_steps: Qualify your causation claims. The HSSIB findings concern IT failures contributing to harm, so say so rather than stating that the malfunction 'led to deaths'. Also distinguish physical-harm failures from data-loss failures, and give a practical rule for when Rachel may ship a known defect.

Check your citations and analogies. Verify the EACE clauses against the code (clause 2.3b concerns competence and experience, not schedules). Replace the CNBC marketing article with a source that supports the Apple, Samsung and Google comparison, and explain why Volkswagen's deliberate defeat devices differ from shipping known defects under time pressure.

Proofread and polish the report. Correct grammatical errors such as 'The economic benefits of could very well be' and 'have her company might go under'. Add at least one figure or table to support your discussion, and make every reference complete and consistent, including a URL for the BBC source.

criteria.C1: Your introduction identifies several ethical issues, including end-user harm, professional responsibility and product quality versus competitiveness, and names the key stakeholders. You also touch on the competitive context of engineering organisations. To reach Excellent, link these issues more explicitly to engineering design and the QA process, and develop each stakeholder's interests, not just their names.
criteria.C2: Your balanced discussion gives three arguments for and three against shipping, and the case against is well developed, drawing on the EACE clauses, the HSSIB case and the Volkswagen case. The arguments for shipping are thinner and partly speculative. To reach Excellent, deepen both sides with objective evidence and make recommendations for several stakeholders, including the chip contract company and the health department.
criteria.C3: Your report flows logically from the for-and-against discussion to the ethical path and then to the conclusion, and the arguments support your recommendation. To reach Excellent, treat all stakeholders systematically and argue claims such as job loss and competitor behaviour rather than asserting them. Clarify the link between your arguments and a practical decision rule.
criteria.C4: You support your arguments with four references, two real-world cases and the EACE code, which gives a reasonable basis for your claims. However, you have little quantitative evidence and no peer-reviewed or technical industry sources, and the CNBC article does not support the competitor claim it is used for. To reach Very good, use references that directly substantiate each argument and add some qualitative or quantitative evidence.
criteria.C5: Your report has a clear structure with abstract, introduction, body, conclusion and references, which serves its purpose well. Several grammatical errors and unclear phrasings reduce fluency, and you have no figures or tables. To reach Good, make the language error-free, include at least one visual element to support your discussion, and ensure your references are complete and consistently formatted.
